passage_1.text:
Mode of transportation affects the travel experience and thus can produce new types of travel writing and perhaps even new "identities." Modes of transportation determine the types and duration of social encounters; affect the organization and passage of space and time; and also affect perception and knowledge, how and what the traveler comes to know and write about. The completion of the first U.S. transcontinental highway during the 1920s for example, inaugurated a new genre of travel literature about the United States, the automotive or road narrative. Such narratives highlight the experiences of mostly male protagonists "discovering themselves" on their journeys, emphasizing the independence of road travel and the value of rural folk traditions.

Travel writing's relationship to empire building as a type of "colonialist discourse"-has drawn the most attention from academicians. Close connections have been observed between European (and American) political, economic, and administrative goals for the colonies and their manifestations in the cultural practice of writing travel books. Travel writers' descriptions of foreign places have been analyzed as attempts to validate, promote, or challenge the ideologies and practices of colonial or imperial domination and expansion. Mary Louise Pratt's study of the genres and conventions of 18th- and 19th-century exploration narratives about South America and Africa (e.g., the "monarch of all I survey" trope) offered ways of thinking about travel writing as embedded within relations of power between metropole and periphery, as did Edward Said's theories of representation and cultural imperialism. Particularly Said's book, Orientalism, helped scholars understand ways in which representations of people in travel texts were intimately bound up with notions of self, in this case, that the Occident defined

itself through essentialist, ethnocentric, and racist representations of the Orient. Said's work became a model for demonstrating cultural forms of imperialism in travel texts, showing how the political, economic, or administrative fact of dominance relies on legitimating discourses such as those articulated through travel writing.

Feminist geographers' studies of travel writing challenge the masculinist history of geography by questioning who and what are relevant subjects of geographic study and, indeed, what counts as geographic knowledge itself. Such questions are worked through ideological constructs that posit men as explorers and women as travelers—or, conversely, men as travelers and women as tied to the home. Studies of Victorian women who were professional travel writers, tourists, wives of colonial administrators, and other (mostly) elite women who wrote narratives about their experiences abroad during the 19th century have been particularly revealing. From a "liberal" feminist perspective, travel presented one means toward female liberation for middle- and upper-class Victorian women. Many studies from the 1970s onward demonstrated the ways in which women's gendered identities were negotiated differently "at home" than they were "away," thereby showing women's self-development through travel. The more recent post structural turn in studies of Victorian travel writing has focused attention on women's diverse and fragmented identities as they narrated their travel experiences, emphasizing women's sense of themselves as women in new locations, but only as they worked through their ties to nation, class, whiteness, and colonial and imperial power structures.

passage_2.text:
Although one of the most contested concepts in political philosophy, human nature is something on which most people seem to agree. By and large, according to Rutger Bregman in his new book Humankind, we have a rather pessimistic view not of ourselves exactly, but of everyone else. We see other people as selfish, untrustworthy and dangerous and therefore we behave towards them with defensiveness and suspicion. This was how the 17th-century philosopher Thomas Hobbes conceived our natural state to be, believing that all that stood between us and violent anarchy was a strong state and firm leadership.

But in following Hobbes, argues Bregman, we ensure that the negative view we have of human nature is reflected back at us. He instead puts his faith in Jean-Jacques Rousseau, the 18th-century French thinker, who famously declared that man was born free and it was civilisation with its coercive powers, social classes and restrictive laws that put him in chains.

Hobbes and Rousseau are seen as the two poles of the human nature argument and it's no surprise that Bregman strongly sides with the Frenchman. He takes Rousseau's intuition and paints a picture of a prelapsarian idyll in which, for the better part of 300,000 years, Homo sapiens lived a fulfilling life in harmony with nature. Then we discovered agriculture and for the next 10,000 years it was all property, war, greed and injustice.

It was abandoning our nomadic lifestyle and then domesticating animals, says Bregman, that brought about infectious diseases such as measles, smallpox, tuberculosis, syphilis, malaria, cholera and plague. This may be true, but what Bregman never really seems to get to grips with is that pathogens were not the only things that grew with agriculture so did the number of humans. It's one thing to maintain friendly relations and a propertyless mode of living when you're 30 or 40 hunter-gatherers following the food. But life becomes a great deal more complex and knowledge far more extensive when there are settlements of many thousands.

"Civilisation has become synonymous with peace and progress and wilderness with war and decline," writes Bregman. "In reality, for most of human existence, it was the other way around." Whereas traditional history depicts the collapse of civilisations as "dark ages” in which everything gets worse, modern scholars, he claims, see them more as a reprieve, in which the enslaved gain their freedom and culture flourishes. Like much else in this book, the truth is probably somewhere between the two stated positions.

In any case, the fear of civilisational collapse, Bregman believes, is unfounded. It's the result of what the Dutch biologist Frans de Waal calls "veneer theory" – the idea that just below the surface, our bestial nature is waiting to break out. There's a great deal of reassuring human decency to be taken from this bold and thought-provoking book and a wealth of evidence in support of the contention that the sense of who we are as a species has been deleteriously distorted. But it seems equally misleading to offer the false choice of Rousseau and Hobbes when, clearly, humanity encompasses both.

passage_3.text:
There is a curious new reality: Human contact is becoming a luxury good. As more screens appear in the lives of the poor, screens are disappearing from the lives of the rich. The richer you are, the more you spend to be off-screen.

The joy at least at first of the internet revolution was its democratic nature. Facebook is the same Facebook whether you are rich or poor. Gmail is the same Gmail. And it's all free. There is something mass market and unappealing about that. And as studies show that time on these advertisement-support platforms is unhealthy, it all starts to seem déclassé, like drinking soda or smoking cigarettes, which wealthy people do less than poor people. The wealthy can afford to opt out of having their data and their attention sold as a product. The poor and middle class don't have the same kind of resources to make that happen.

Screen exposure starts young. And children who spent more than two hours a day looking at a screen got lower scores on thinking and language tests, according to early results of a landmark study on brain development of more than 11,000 children that the National Institutes of Health is supporting. Most disturbingly, the study is finding that the brains of children who spend a lot of time on screens are different. For some kids, there is premature thinning of their cerebral cortex. In adults, one study found an association between screen time and depression.

Tech companies worked hard to get public schools to buy into programs that required schools to have one laptop per student, arguing that it would better prepare children for their screen- based future. But this idea isn't how the people who actually build the screen-based future raise their own children. In Silicon Valley, time on screens is increasingly seen as unhealthy. Here, the popular elementary school is the local Waldorf School, which promises a back-to- nature, nearly screen-free education. So as wealthy kids are growing up with less screen time, poor kids are growing up with more. How comfortable someone is with human engagement could become a new class marker.

Human contact is, of course, not exactly like organic food But with screen time, there has been a concerted effort on the part of Silicon Valley behemoths to confuse the public. The poor and the middle class are told that screens are good and important for them and their children. There are fleets of psychologists and neuroscientists on staff at big tech companies working to hook eyes and minds to the screen as fast as possible and for as long as possible. And so human contact is rare.

There is a small movement to pass a "right to disconnect" bill, which would allow workers to turn their phones off, but for now a worker can be punished for going offline and not being available. There is also the reality that in our culture of increasing isolation, in which so many of the traditional gathering places and social structures have disappeared, screens are filling a crucial void.

passage_4.text:
I've been following the economic crisis for more than two years now. I began working on the subject as part of the background to a novel, and soon realized that I had stumbled across the most interesting story I've ever found. While I was beginning to work on it, the British bank Northern Rock blew up, and it became clear that, as I wrote at the time, "If our laws are not extended to control the new kinds of super-powerful, super-complex, and potentially super- risky investment vehicles, they will one day cause a financial disaster of global-systemic proportions." I was both right and too late, because all the groundwork for the crisis had already been done though the sluggishness of the world's governments, in not preparing for the great unraveling of autumn 2008, was then and still is stupefying. But this is the first reason why I wrote this book: because what's happened is extraordinarily interesting. It is an absolutely amazing story, full of human interest and drama, one whose byways of mathematics, economics, and psychology are both central to the story of the last decades and mysteriously unknown to the general public. We have heard a lot about "the two cultures" of science and the arts we heard a particularly large amount

about it in 2009, because it was the fiftieth anniversary of the speech during which C. P. Snow first used the phrase. But I'm not sure the idea of a huge gap between science and the arts is as true as it was half a century ago it's certainly true, for instance, that a general reader who wants to pick up an education in the fundamentals of science will find it easier than ever before. It seems to me that there is a much bigger gap between the world of finance and that of the general public and that there is a need to narrow that gap, if the financial industry is not to be a kind of priesthood, administering to its own mysteries and feared and resented by the rest of us. Many bright, literate people have no idea about all sorts of economic basics, of a type that financial insiders take as elementary facts of how the world works. I am an outsider to finance and economics, and my hope is that I can talk across that gulf.

My need to understand is the same as yours, whoever you are. That's one of the strangest ironies of this story: after decades in which the ideology of the Western world was personally and economically individualistic, we've suddenly been hit by a crisis which shows in the starkest terms that whether we like it or not and there are large parts of it that you would have to be crazy to like we're all in this together. The aftermath of the crisis is going to dominate the economics and politics of our societies for at least a decade to come and perhaps longer.

questions.question_text: According to the passage, Said's book, "Orientalism":

options.label: A
options.text: explained the difference between the representation of people and the actual fact.

options.label: B
options.text: illustrated how narrow minded and racist westerners were.

options.label: C
options.text: argued that cultural imperialism was more significant than colonial domination.

options.label: D
options.text: demonstrated how cultural imperialism was used to justify colonial domination

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what Said's "Orientalism" specifically did according to the passage. Let us trace through the key information step by step.

From passage: "Said's work became a model for demonstrating cultural forms of imperialism in travel texts, showing how the political, economic, or administrative fact of dominance relies on legitimating discourses such as those articulated through travel writing."

The passage tells us Said showed how cultural imperialism (like racist travel writing) was used to support and justify actual colonial power (political and economic dominance).

Think of it this way: Colonial powers needed to justify their dominance -> They used cultural means (like travel writing with racist ideas) -> This cultural imperialism made colonial domination seem legitimate and right.

🟠 Option 1 -> scope-error -> focuses on representation vs. facts, but passage shows Said focused on how representations justified dominance, not just compared them to reality

🟠 Option 2 -> partial-truth -> yes, passage mentions racist representations, but misses Said's main point about how these served to justify colonial power

🟠 Option 3 -> reverses-relationship -> passage shows cultural imperialism supported colonial domination, not that it was more important than it

🟢 Option 4 -> matches perfectly -> captures exactly what passage says: cultural imperialism (legitimating discourses) was used to justify colonial domination (political/economic dominance)

The key insight is that Said didn't just point out racism - he showed how this cultural racism served a purpose: making colonial power seem justified and natural.

questions.question_text: From the passage, it can be inferred that scholars argue that Victorian women experienced self-development through their travels because:

options.label: A
options.text: their identity was redefined when they were away from home.

options.label: B
options.text: they were on a quest to discover their diverse identities.

options.label: C
options.text: they were from the progressive middle- and upper-classes of society.

options.label: D
options.text: they developed a feminist perspective of the world

questions.explanation_text:
The answer lies in the last paragraph where it explains the scholarly findings about women's travel experiences.

From passage: "Many studies from the 1970s onward demonstrated the ways in which women's gendered identities were negotiated differently 'at home' than they were 'away,' thereby showing women's self-development through travel."

The passage shows a clear cause-and-effect: Women's identities were different at home vs away -> this led to self-development. The key insight is that being away from home allowed them to negotiate their identities differently.

🟠 Option 2 -> context-shift -> mentions "quest to discover diverse identities" but passage talks about diverse identities in a different context (post-structural analysis), not as the reason for self-development

🟠 Option 3 -> irrelevant -> describes who these women were (their social class) but doesn't explain why they experienced self-development through travel

🟠 Option 4 -> scope-error -> confuses the feminist scholarly perspective used to study these women with the women's own personal development

🟢 Option 1 is correct -> directly captures the core reason: their identity changed/was redefined when away from home, which is exactly what the passage says led to self-development

The confusion here might be between options 1 and 2, but option 2 talks about a "quest" which suggests they were actively seeking diverse identities, while the passage simply says their identities were negotiated differently in different places.

questions.question_text:
From the passage, we can infer that feminist scholars' understanding of the experiences of Victorian women travellers is

influenced by all of the following EXCEPT scholars':

options.label: A
options.text: awareness of gender issues in Victorian society

options.label: B
options.text: awareness of the ways in which identity is formed

options.label: C
options.text: perspective that they bring to their research

options.label: D
options.text: knowledge of class tensions in Victorian society

questions.explanation_text:
The key is in the last paragraph about feminist geographers.we need to check what the passage actually says influences their research vs what it doesn't mention.

From passage: "From a 'liberal' feminist perspective, travel presented one means toward female liberation for middle- and upper-class Victorian women. Many studies from the 1970s onward demonstrated the ways in which women's gendered identities were negotiated differently 'at home' than they were 'away'... The more recent post structural turn in studies of Victorian travel writing has focused attention on women's diverse and fragmented identities as they narrated their travel experiences, emphasizing women's sense of themselves as women in new locations, but only as they worked through their ties to nation, class, whiteness, and colonial and imperial power structures."

My thought process -> The passage talks about what shapes these scholars' understanding.we need to find what's missing from their list of influences.

🟠 Option 1 -> clearly mentioned -> passage talks about "gendered identities" and gender constructs throughout

🟠 Option 2 -> clearly mentioned -> passage discusses "diverse and fragmented identities" and how identity forms through travel

🟠 Option 3 -> clearly mentioned -> passage mentions "liberal feminist perspective" and "post structural turn" showing different research approaches

🟢 Option 4 is correct -> not mentioned as influence -> while passage mentions "class" (middle/upper-class women), it never talks about class tensions or class conflict influencing scholars' understanding

The passage mentions class only as a descriptor (middle-class, upper-class women) but never suggests that knowledge of class tensions shapes how feminist scholars understand these women's experiences. The other three options are all directly stated as influences on scholarly understanding.

questions.question_text: American travel literature of the 1920s:

options.label: A
options.text: developed the male protagonists' desire for independence.

options.label: B
options.text: showed participation in local traditions.

options.label: C
options.text: presented travellers' discovery of their identity as different from others.

options.label: D
options.text: celebrated the freedom that travel gives.

questions.explanation_text:
Let us trace through the first paragraph where this is discussed.

From passage: "The completion of the first U.S. transcontinental highway during the 1920s for example, inaugurated a new genre of travel literature about the United States, the automotive or road narrative. Such narratives highlight the experiences of mostly male protagonists "discovering themselves" on their journeys, emphasizing the independence of road travel and the value of rural folk traditions."

The passage tells us what these 1920s road narratives actually did -> they emphasized the independence of road travel. When literature emphasizes something positive like independence, it's essentially celebrating that concept.

Key distinction: The passage talks about what the literature showed or emphasized, not what it developed in people.

Elimination process:

🟠 Option 1 -> scope-error -> Says literature "developed" desire for independence, but passage only says it "emphasized the independence of road travel." Developing desire vs. emphasizing existing independence are different things.

🟠 Option 2 -> degree-error -> Says "participation" in traditions, but passage says "value of rural folk traditions." Valuing something and participating in it are different actions.

🟠 Option 3 -> partial-truth -> Right about discovering identity, but adds "as different from others" which isn't in the passage. The text just says "discovering themselves" period.

🟢 Option 4 -> correct -> "Celebrated the freedom that travel gives" matches "emphasizing the independence of road travel." Independence and freedom mean basically the same thing, and emphasizing something positive = celebrating it.

The key is recognizing that emphasizing independence = celebrating freedom. Same concept, different words.

questions.question_text: From the passage, we can infer that travel writing is most similar to:

options.label: A
options.text: historical fiction

options.label: B
options.text: political journalism

options.label: C
options.text: feminist writing

options.label: D
options.text: autobiographical writing

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what travel writing shares most characteristics with based on the passage's description.

The passage shows travel writing as personal accounts where people write about their own experiences. Key clues:

From passage: "Such narratives highlight the experiences of mostly male protagonists 'discovering themselves' on their journeys"

From passage: "women who wrote narratives about their experiences abroad"

The thought process -> travel writing = people writing about their own travel experiences -> this matches autobiographical writing (writing about your own life experiences)

Elimination process:

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> historical fiction is made-up stories set in the past, but travel writing describes real personal experiences, not fictional ones

🔴 Option 2 -> context-shift -> political journalism reports on political events objectively, but travel writing focuses on personal experiences and self-discovery during travel

🟠 Option 3 -> partial-truth -> while the passage discusses feminist perspectives on travel writing, travel writing itself isn't necessarily feminist writing - it's just personal accounts that feminists study

🟢 Option 4 is correct -> autobiographical writing means writing about your own life experiences, which perfectly matches how the passage describes travel writing as people narrating their own travel experiences and discoveries about themselves

The passage consistently shows travel writing as first-person accounts of personal experiences, making it most similar to autobiographical writing.

questions.question_text: The author has differing views from Bregman regarding:

options.label: A
options.text: a civilised society being coercive and unjust.

options.label: B
options.text: a property-less mode of living being socially harmonious.

options.label: C
options.text: the role of agriculture in the advancement of knowledge.

options.label: D
options.text: the role of pathogens in the spread of infectious diseases.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find where the author disagrees with Bregman's views. Let us trace through the passage to spot these disagreements.

The author presents Bregman's views but then offers critiques. The key is finding where the author says "but" or "however" or similar words that signal disagreement.

Process: Find Bregman's views -> Look for author's counter-arguments -> Match with options

From passage: "But it seems equally misleading to offer the false choice of Rousseau and Hobbes when, clearly, humanity encompasses both."

This shows the author thinks Bregman is wrong to present civilization as simply bad (Rousseau's view). Bregman follows Rousseau who said civilization with its "coercive powers, social classes and restrictive laws" put humans "in chains."

Thought process: Author disagrees with Bregman's black-and-white view -> Bregman sees civilization as purely coercive/unjust -> Author thinks this is too simple -> Reality includes both good and bad aspects

🟢 Option 1 -> Correct -> Author disagrees with Bregman's view that civilized society is simply coercive and unjust. Author thinks humanity "encompasses both" good and bad.

🟠 Option 2 -> partial-truth -> Author does question this indirectly when discussing settlement complexity, but it's not the main disagreement.

🟠 Option 3 -> scope-error -> Author mentions knowledge advancement but doesn't really disagree with Bregman about this specifically.

🔴 Option 4 -> irrelevant -> Author actually agrees with Bregman here, saying "This may be true" about the pathogen argument.

Key insight: When authors use phrases like "false choice" or "equally misleading," they're rejecting the entire framework being presented, not just details within it.

questions.question_text: According to the author, the main reason why Bregman contrasts life in pre- agricultural societies with agricultural societies is to:

options.label: A
options.text: make the argument that an environmentally conscious lifestyle is a more harmonious way of living.

options.label: B
options.text: bolster his argument that people are basically decent, but progress as we know it can make them selfish.

options.label: C
options.text: advocate the promotion of less complex societies as a basis for greater security and prosperity.

options.label: D
options.text: highlight the enormous impact that settled farming had on population growth.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find why Bregman contrasts pre-agricultural vs agricultural societies. The key is understanding his bigger argument about human nature.

Step-by-step thought process:

First, we need to see what Bregman's main argument is -> He sides with Rousseau (humans naturally good) over Hobbes (humans naturally bad)

Then we look at how he supports this argument -> He contrasts two time periods to show humans were good before civilization corrupted them

From passage: "He takes Rousseau's intuition and paints a picture of a prelapsarian idyll in which, for the better part of 300,000 years, Homo sapiens lived a fulfilling life in harmony with nature. Then we discovered agriculture and for the next 10,000 years it was all property, war, greed and injustice."

The contrast serves his bigger point -> Natural humans = good, Civilized humans = corrupted by progress

Option analysis:

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> focuses only on "environmentally conscious lifestyle" but misses the bigger point about human nature vs civilization

🟢 Option 2 -> captures the essence -> perfectly matches Bregman's argument that humans start decent but civilization/progress corrupts them into selfishness

🟠 Option 3 -> overstates -> suggests Bregman is advocating we return to simpler societies, but he's just making a philosophical point about what corrupts human nature

🔴 Option 4 -> misses the point -> population growth is mentioned but it's actually the author's criticism of Bregman, not Bregman's main reason for the contrast

The contrast directly supports Bregman's Rousseau-inspired view that we're naturally decent but progress makes us selfish.

questions.question_text: According to the passage, the "collapse of civilisations" is viewed by Bregman as:

options.label: A
options.text: a time that enables changes in societies and cultures.

options.label: B
options.text: a sign of regression in society's trajectory.

options.label: C
options.text: a temporary phase which can be rectified by social action.

options.label: D
options.text: resulting from a breakdown in the veneer of human nature.

questions.explanation_text:
To solve this question,we need to find what Bregman specifically believes about civilizational collapse, not what others think.

The passage contrasts two views -> traditional history vs modern scholars (who Bregman agrees with)

Traditional view: collapse = "dark ages" where everything gets worse

Bregman's view (via modern scholars): collapse = something positive

From passage: "Whereas traditional history depicts the collapse of civilisations as 'dark ages' in which everything gets worse, modern scholars, he claims, see them more as a reprieve, in which the enslaved gain their freedom and culture flourishes."

Key insight -> Bregman sees collapse as a reprieve (relief/break) where:

  • Enslaved people gain freedom
  • Culture flourishes

This means collapse = positive change in societies and cultures

🟢 Option 1 -> correct -> captures Bregman's view perfectly. "Time that enables changes" matches with "enslaved gain freedom and culture flourishes"

🔴 Option 2 -> opposite-view -> this describes the traditional view (regression/dark ages), not Bregman's view

🟠 Option 3 -> context-shift -> treats collapse as something bad needing fixes. But Bregman sees it as good (reprieve, freedom, flourishing)

🟠 Option 4 -> scope-error -> "veneer theory" is mentioned but relates to fears about collapse, not Bregman's actual definition of what collapse is

The key trick here: don't confuse Bregman's positive view of collapse with the traditional negative view. He's arguing collapse is actually beneficial!

questions.question_text: None of the following views is expressed in the passage EXCEPT that:

options.label: A
options.text: Bregman agrees with Hobbes that firm leadership is needed to ensure property rights and regulate strife.

options.label: B
options.text: Hobbes and Rousseau disagreed on the fundamental nature of humans, but both believed in the need for a strong state.

options.label: C
options.text: the author of the review believes in the veneer theory of human nature.

options.label: D
options.text: most people agree with Hobbes' pessimistic view of human nature as being intrinsically untrustworthy and selfish.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find which view IS expressed in the passage (since it asks for the EXCEPT).

The key is to look for direct evidence in the passage for each option. Since this is an EXCEPT question, I'm looking for the one that IS actually mentioned.

From passage: "By and large, according to Rutger Bregman in his new book Humankind, we have a rather pessimistic view not of ourselves exactly, but of everyone else. We see other people as selfish, untrustworthy and dangerous... This was how the 17th-century philosopher Thomas Hobbes conceived our natural state to be."

Process: Most people have pessimistic view of others -> they see others as selfish/untrustworthy -> this matches Hobbes' view -> so most people agree with Hobbes' pessimistic view

🔴 Option 1 -> contradicts passage -> Bregman clearly sides with Rousseau, not Hobbes. Passage says "He instead puts his faith in Jean-Jacques Rousseau" and "strongly sides with the Frenchman"

🔴 Option 2 -> partial-truth -> They disagreed on human nature (correct), but passage never says Rousseau believed in strong state. Actually suggests opposite since Rousseau thought civilization put man "in chains"

🔴 Option 3 -> scope-error -> Passage mentions veneer theory as what Frans de Waal calls it, and what Bregman discusses, but doesn't say the review author believes in it

🟢 Option 4 -> directly stated -> Passage clearly says most people ("by and large") have pessimistic view of others as selfish/untrustworthy, which matches exactly what Hobbes believed about human nature

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about the negative effects of screen time is the author least likely to endorse?

options.label: A
options.text: It can cause depression in viewers.

options.label: B
options.text: It is designed to be addictive.

options.label: C
options.text: It increases human contact as it fills an isolation void.

options.label: D
options.text: It is shown to have adverse effects on young children's learning.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find which statement the author would least likely endorse about screen time's negative effects. This means I'm looking for either a positive effect or something the author doesn't support.

Let us trace through the passage to understand the author's stance on screen time effects:

From passage: "In adults, one study found an association between screen time and depression" and "children who spent more than two hours a day looking at a screen got lower scores on thinking and language tests"

The author clearly presents screen time as harmful -> depression, learning problems, brain changes -> wealthy people avoid it -> poor people get more exposed to it.

The key insight is the word "negative effects" in the question.we need to find what the author would not consider a negative effect, or what contradicts the author's negative view.

From passage: "There is also the reality that in our culture of increasing isolation, in which so many of the traditional gathering places and social structures have disappeared, screens are filling a crucial void."

But the author also says -> "human contact is rare" and "Human contact is becoming a luxury good" -> so screens aren't really increasing genuine human contact.

🔴 Option 1 -> directly supported -> author cites study linking screen time to depression

🔴 Option 2 -> directly supported -> author mentions tech companies using "psychologists and neuroscientists...to hook eyes and minds"

🟢 Option 3 -> contradicts author's view -> while author mentions screens "fill a void," the overall message is that screens reduce human contact and make it a "luxury good"

🔴 Option 4 -> directly supported -> author cites study showing lower test scores and brain changes in children

Option 3 presents something that sounds positive (increasing human contact), but the author's entire argument is that screens are making real human contact rarer and more expensive. The author wouldn't endorse the idea that screens increase human contact.

questions.question_text: The author is least likely to agree with the view that the increase in screen-time is fuelled by the fact that:

options.label: A
options.text: screens provide social contact in an increasingly isolating world.

options.label: B
options.text: with falling costs, people are streaming more content on their devices.

options.label: C
options.text: some workers face punitive action if they are not online.

options.label: D
options.text: there is a growth in computer-based teaching in public schools

questions.explanation_text:
Let us trace through the passage to see what factors the author actually mentions for increased screen time:

The passage discusses several reasons for more screen time -> social isolation filling a void -> work requirements forcing people online -> schools pushing laptop programs. Butwe need to check if cost factors are mentioned anywhere.

From passage: "There is also the reality that in our culture of increasing isolation, in which so many of the traditional gathering places and social structures have disappeared, screens are filling a crucial void."

From passage: "a worker can be punished for going offline and not being available"

From passage: "Tech companies worked hard to get public schools to buy into programs that required schools to have one laptop per student"

The passage mentions that Facebook and Gmail are "free" but doesn't connect falling device costs to increased usage. The author focuses on other drivers entirely.

🟢 Option 1 -> directly supported -> passage explicitly says screens fill social voids in isolated culture

🔴 Option 2 -> not mentioned -> passage never discusses falling costs or streaming as drivers of screen time increase

🟢 Option 3 -> directly supported -> passage clearly states workers can be punished for going offline

🟢 Option 4 -> directly supported -> passage mentions tech companies pushing laptop programs in schools

The confusion here might be that options 1, 3, and 4 all seem reasonable and are backed by the text. But option 2 introduces an economic factor (falling costs) that the author simply doesn't discuss as a reason for increased screen time. The author focuses on social, workplace, and educational pressures instead.

questions.question_text: The author claims that Silicon Valley tech companies have tried to "confuse the public" by:

options.label: A
options.text: promoting screen time in public schools while opting for a screen-free education for their own children.

options.label: B
options.text: developing new work-efficiency programmes while lobbying for the "right to disconnect" bill.

options.label: C
options.text: concealing the findings of psychologists and neuroscientists on screen-time use from the public.

options.label: D
options.text: pushing for greater privacy while working with advertisement-support platforms to mine data.

questions.explanation_text:
Step 1: Look for the word "confuse" in the passage -> find what comes right after it.

Step 2: Find examples of tech companies saying one thing but doing another -> this creates confusion.

From passage: "Tech companies worked hard to get public schools to buy into programs that required schools to have one laptop per student... But this idea isn't how the people who actually build the screen-based future raise their own children. In Silicon Valley... the popular elementary school is the local Waldorf School, which promises a back-to-nature, nearly screen-free education."

From passage: "The poor and the middle class are told that screens are good and important for them and their children."

Thought process:

Tech companies tell public schools -> screens are great for kids -> push laptop programs

BUT same tech people -> send their own kids -> to screen-free schools

This contradiction -> creates confusion -> classic "do as I say, not as I do"

🟢 Option 1 -> correct -> captures the exact contradiction described: promoting screens for public schools vs choosing screen-free education for their own kids

🔴 Option 2 -> irrelevant -> passage mentions "right to disconnect" as a small movement, not something tech companies lobby for

🔴 Option 3 -> scope-error -> passage says they hire psychologists to hook people to screens, not that they're hiding research findings

🔴 Option 4 -> not-mentioned -> privacy vs data mining contradiction isn't discussed in this context

The confusion comes from the hypocrisy -> they push screens on everyone else's kids while protecting their own kids from screens.

questions.question_text: The statement "The richer you are, the more you spend to be off-screen" is supported by which other line from the passage?

options.label: A
options.text: "How comfortable someone is with human engagement could become a new class marker."

options.label: B
options.text: screens are filling a crucial void."

options.label: C
options.text: studies show that time on these advertisement-support platforms is unhealthy.

options.label: D
options.text: "Gmail is the same Gmail. And it's all free."

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "Human contact is becoming a luxury good"

This opening line sets up the main idea -> rich people can buy their way out of screen time while poor people cannot. The passage shows wealthy people paying for screen-free schools, opting out of data collection, and choosing human interaction over digital platforms.

Now we need to find which option best supports this "spending to be off-screen" concept:

🟢 Option 1 is correct -> "How comfortable someone is with human engagement could become a new class marker" -> directly connects social class with human contact (being off-screen) -> shows that being comfortable with real human interaction will separate rich from poor

🔴 Option 2 -> irrelevant -> "screens are filling a crucial void" -> talks about why people use screens, not about rich people avoiding them -> doesn't support spending to be off-screen

🔴 Option 3 -> context-shift -> "studies show that time on these platforms is unhealthy" -> explains why people might want to avoid screens but says nothing about rich people spending money to do so -> missing the wealth connection

🔴 Option 4 -> contradicts -> "Gmail is the same Gmail. And it's all free" -> talks about things being free, which goes against the idea of spending money to be off-screen -> opposite direction

The key insight: Option 1 connects human engagement (off-screen behavior) with class differences, which directly supports the idea that rich people spend money to avoid screens while poor people cannot.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following best captures the main argument of the last paragraph of the passage?

options.label: A
options.text: Whoever you are, you would be crazy to think that there is no crisis.

options.label: B
options.text: The aftermath of the crisis will strengthen the central ideology of individualism in the Western world.

options.label: C
options.text: The ideology of individualism must be set aside in order to deal with the crisis.

options.label: D
options.text: In the decades to come, other ideologies will emerge in the aftermath of the crisis.

questions.explanation_text:
The author talks about irony - something surprising or opposite of what you'd expect. He says after decades of individualism, the crisis shows "we're all in this together."

From passage: "That's one of the strangest ironies of this story: after decades in which the ideology of the Western world was personally and economically individualistic, we've suddenly been hit by a crisis which shows in the starkest terms that whether we like it or not... we're all in this together."

Thought process: Decades of individualism -> Crisis hits -> Shows we need to work together -> Individualism doesn't work anymore

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> focuses on denying crisis exists, but passage isn't about people denying the crisis - it's about what the crisis teaches us

🔴 Option 2 -> opposite-meaning -> says crisis will strengthen individualism, but passage says crisis shows individualism doesn't work - completely backward

🟢 Option 3 -> correct -> captures the main point that individualistic thinking must be set aside because crisis shows "we're all in this together"

🔴 Option 4 -> scope-error -> talks about new ideologies emerging, but passage only says individualism doesn't work - doesn't predict what will replace it

Key insight: The author isn't predicting the future or talking about crisis denial. He's pointing out that individualism (the old way) doesn't work for this crisis because everyone is affected together.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following, if true, would be an accurate inference from the first sentence of the passage?

options.label: A
options.text: The author's preoccupation with the economic crisis is not less than two years old.

options.label: B
options.text: The economic crisis outlasted the author's preoccupation with it.

options.label: C
options.text: The author has witnessed many economic crises by travelling a lot for two years.

options.label: D
options.text: The author is preoccupied with the economic crisis because he is being followed.

questions.explanation_text:
Step 1: Find the key sentence

The question asks about the first sentence specifically. Let's isolate it:

From passage: "I've been following the economic crisis for more than two years now."

Step 2: Understand what "inference" means

An inference is something we can logically conclude from the given information. We need to find what must be true based on this sentence.

Step 3: Break down the sentence

"More than two years" → This means at least two years, but could be longer.

Option Analysis Process:

🟢 Option 1 → Correct → "not less than two years old" means the same as "more than two years" (double negative = positive)

🔴 Option 2 → scope-error → talks about when crisis ended vs. author's interest - first sentence gives no info about endings

🔴 Option 3 → irrelevant → mentions "many crises" and "travelling" - first sentence mentions only one crisis and no travel

🔴 Option 4 → misinterpretation → confuses "following" (studying/tracking) with "being followed" (chased by someone)

Key insight: "More than two years" is the same as saying "not less than two years." Both mean the time period is at least two years or longer.

Quick elimination tip: In inference questions, stick strictly to what the sentence actually says. Options 2, 3, and 4 all add new information not present in the first sentence.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following, if false, could be seen as supporting the author's claims?

options.label: A
options.text: Most people are yet to gain any real understanding of the workings of the financial world.

options.label: B
options.text: The global economic crisis lasted for more than two years.

options.label: C
options.text: The huge gap between science and the arts has steadily narrowed over time.

options.label: D
options.text: The economic crisis was not a failure of collective action to rectify economic problems.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find which statement, when made false, would support what the author believes.

Step 1: Find the author's key claims first -> Government was slow to act, there's a gap between finance world and public, we need collective action

Step 2: Test each option by making it false -> See which one strengthens author's argument

From passage: "though the sluggishness of the world's governments, in not preparing for the great unraveling of autumn 2008, was then and still is stupefying"

The author clearly criticizes governments for being slow and unprepared -> This shows he thinks the crisis WAS a failure of collective action.

🟠 Option 1 -> If false: "Most people DO understand finance" -> This would weaken author's claim about the big gap between finance and public

🟠 Option 2 -> If false: "Crisis lasted less than 2 years" -> Doesn't connect to author's main arguments about government failure or collective action

🟠 Option 3 -> If false: "Science-arts gap hasn't narrowed" -> Author actually agrees the gap has narrowed, so making this false contradicts him

🟢 Option 4 -> If false: "The crisis WAS a failure of collective action" -> This directly supports author's criticism of government sluggishness and unpreparedness

Key insight: When we make Option 4 false, we get "The crisis WAS a failure of collective action" - which perfectly matches the author's complaint about government sluggishness.

questions.question_text: All of the following, if true, could be seen as supporting the arguments in the passage, EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: The difficulty with understanding financial matters is that they have become so arcane.

options.label: B
options.text: Economic crises could be averted by changing prevailing ideologies and beliefs.

options.label: C
options.text: The story of the economic crisis is also one about international relations, global financial security, and mass psychology.

options.label: D
options.text: The failure of economic systems does not necessarily mean the failure of their ideologies.

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "after decades in which the ideology of the Western world was personally and economically individualistic, we've suddenly been hit by a crisis which shows in the starkest terms that...we're all in this together."

The author clearly connects the individualistic ideology -> economic crisis. This suggests ideologies can cause problems, not that they're separate from system failures.

Elimination Process:

Students often get confused between options 2 and 4 here. 🟢 Option 1 -> supported -> passage says "gap between finance and general public" + "Many bright, literate people have no idea about economic basics" = financial matters are arcane/difficult

🟢 Option 2 -> supported -> author links individualistic ideology to crisis, implying different ideologies might prevent crises

🟢 Option 3 -> supported -> passage mentions "byways of mathematics, economics, and psychology" + "global-systemic proportions" = matches international relations, security, psychology

🔴 Option 4 -> contradicts passage -> author directly blames individualistic ideology for contributing to economic crisis. This option says ideologies and system failures are unrelated, but passage shows they ARE connected

The key insight: Author argues ideology caused the crisis. Option 4 says ideology and system failure are unrelated. This directly contradicts the passage's main argument about how individualistic thinking led to our current mess.

Option 4 is correct because it's the only one that goes against what the passage argues.

questions.question_text: According to the passage, the author is likely to be supportive of which one of the following programmes?

options.label: A
options.text: An educational curriculum that promotes economic research.

options.label: B
options.text: Economic policies that are more sensitively calibrated to the fluctuations of the market.

options.label: C
options.text: An educational curriculum that promotes developing financial literacy in the masses.

options.label: D
options.text: The complete nationalisation of all financial institutions.

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "It seems to me that there is a much bigger gap between the world of finance and that of the general public and that there is a need to narrow that gap, if the financial industry is not to be a kind of priesthood, administering to its own mysteries and feared and resented by the rest of us."

Author's concern -> finance world is like a priesthood (exclusive club) -> general public doesn't understand basic economics -> this gap needs to be narrowed

From passage: "Many bright, literate people have no idea about all sorts of economic basics, of a type that financial insiders take as elementary facts of how the world works."

Author's solution -> educate the masses about finance basics -> make finance knowledge accessible to everyone -> bridge the gap

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> focuses on creating researchers, not educating masses. Author wants to teach general public, not create more experts.

🔴 Option 2 -> irrelevant -> about policy-making, not education. Author's concern is knowledge gap, not market policies.

🟢 Option 3 -> correct -> perfectly matches author's goal. "Financial literacy in masses" = narrowing the gap between finance world and general public.

🔴 Option 4 -> extreme/irrelevant -> nationalizing banks isn't mentioned anywhere. Author talks about education, not changing ownership.

Key insight: Author sees the problem as ignorance, not bad institutions. His solution is education, not restructuring.

questions.question_text:
Five jumbled up sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in the number of that sentence as your answer.

  1. Machine learning models are prone to learning human-like biases from the training data that feeds these algorithms.
  2. Hate speech detection is part of the on-going effort against oppressive and abusive language on social media.
  3. The current automatic detection models miss out on something vital: context.
  4. It uses complex algorithms to flag racist or violent speech faster and better than human beings alone.
  5. For instance, algorithms struggle to determine if group identifiers like "gay" or "black" are used in offensive or prejudiced ways because they're trained on imbalanced datasets with unusually high rates of hate speech.
questions.explanation_text:
Step 1: Find the main topic -> All sentences talk about hate speech detection systems, butwe need to see which four connect smoothly.

Step 2: Look for the flow of ideas -> Sentences should build on each other or connect logically.

From passage: "Machine learning models are prone to learning human-like biases" and "For instance, algorithms struggle to determine if group identifiers like 'gay' or 'black' are used in offensive ways"

The main story here: Hate speech detection exists -> It uses algorithms -> But it has bias problems -> Here's an example of bias.

Thought Process:

Sentence 2 -> introduces hate speech detection

Sentence 4 -> explains how it works (algorithms)

Sentence 1 -> explains the main problem (bias from training data)

Sentence 5 -> gives a specific example of this bias problem

These four connect perfectly: what it is -> how it works -> what's wrong -> example

Sentence 3 -> talks about missing "context" which is a totally different issue than bias

Why Sentence 3 is the odd one out:

🔴 Sentence 3 is incorrect -> scope-error -> introduces "context" as a problem, but the other four sentences focus specifically on bias issues, not context issues. It shifts to a different type of problem that doesn't connect with the bias discussion.

The coherent paragraph flows: hate speech detection systems (2) use complex algorithms (4) but suffer from human-like biases in training data (1), for example with words like "gay" or "black" (5).

Sentence 3 brings up context understanding, which is unrelated to the bias theme running through the other four sentences.

Answer: 3

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Aesthetic political representation urges us to realize that 'the representative has autonomy with regard to the people represented' but autonomy then is not an excuse to abandon one's responsibility. Aesthetic autonomy requires cultivation of 'disinterestedness' on the part of actors which is not indifference. To have disinterestedness, that is, to have comportment towards the beautiful that is devoid of all ulterior references to use requires a kind of aesthetic commitment; it is the liberation of ourselves for the release of what has proper worth only in itself.

options.label: A
options.text: Aesthetic political representation advocates autonomy for the representatives drawing from disinterestedness, which itself is different from indifference.

options.label: B
options.text: Aesthetic political representation advocates autonomy for the representatives manifested through disinterestedness which itself is different from indifference.

options.label: C
options.text: Disinterestedness is different from indifference as the former means a non-subjective evaluation of things which is what constitutes aesthetic political representation.

options.label: D
options.text: Disinterestedness, as distinct from indifference, is the basis of political representation.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what aesthetic political representation is really about. From passage: "The representative has autonomy with regard to the people represented' but autonomy then is not an excuse to abandon one's responsibility. Aesthetic autonomy requires cultivation of 'disinterestedness' on the part of actors which is not indifference."

The passage moves through this logic: Representatives get autonomy -> but must stay responsible -> this needs disinterestedness -> disinterestedness ≠ indifference.

Think of it like this: A judge (representative) can make independent decisions (autonomy) but can't ignore their duty to be fair (responsibility). They need to be unbiased (disinterested) but still care about justice (not indifferent).

Now let's check each option:

🟢 Option 1 -> correct -> captures the main relationship: aesthetic political representation gives autonomy that "draws from" disinterestedness, and clarifies disinterestedness ≠ indifference

🟠 Option 2 -> close but less precise -> says autonomy is "manifested through" disinterestedness instead of "drawing from" it. The passage shows disinterestedness as a requirement for autonomy, not just how it shows up

🔴 Option 3 -> scope-error -> flips the relationship. Says disinterestedness "constitutes" aesthetic political representation, but passage shows aesthetic political representation needs disinterestedness, not that disinterestedness makes it

🔴 Option 4 -> too broad -> drops "aesthetic" and talks about all "political representation." This misses the specific concept the passage discusses

The confusion here is between Options 1 and 2. Both mention autonomy and the disinterestedness vs indifference point. But Option 1 says autonomy "draws from" disinterestedness (like getting strength from it), while Option 2 says it's "manifested through" it (like being shown by it). The passage says autonomy "requires" disinterestedness, so Option 1's "drawing from" better captures this dependency.

questions.question_text:
Five jumbled up sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in the number of that sentence as your answer.

  1. The logic of displaying one's inner qualities through outward appearance was based on a distinction between being a woman and being feminine.

2.'Appearance' became a signifier of conduct - to look was to be and conformity to the feminine ideal was measured by how well women could use the tools of the fashion and beauty industries.

  1. The makeover-centric media sets out subtly and not-so-subtly, 'good' and 'bad' ways to be a woman, layering these over inequalities of race and class.
  2. The denigration of working-class women and women of colour often centres on their perceived failure to embody feminine beauty.

5.'Woman' was considered a biological category, but femininity was a 'process' by which women became specific kinds of women.
questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "The logic of displaying one's inner qualities through outward appearance was based on a distinction between being a woman and being feminine."

The core theme -> distinction between "woman" (biological) vs "femininity" (a process you perform)

Let us trace the logical flow:

  • Sentence 5 sets up the basic distinction -> woman = biological, femininity = process
  • Sentence 1 builds on this -> explains the logic of showing inner qualities through looks
  • Sentence 2 continues -> appearance became the measure of conduct and conformity
  • Sentence 4 shows consequence -> those who failed this standard (working-class women, women of color) got criticized

But sentence 3 -> talks about media's role in setting these standards

Think like this: The main story is about a concept (woman vs femininity) -> how it worked (appearance as measure) -> what happened to those who didn't meet it (denigration).

Sentence 3 shifts focus to who creates these standards (media) rather than continuing the explanation of the concept itself.

🟢 Option 3 is the odd one out -> context-shift -> while related, it moves from explaining the woman/femininity distinction and its effects to discussing who perpetuates these ideas (media), which breaks the conceptual flow of the other 4 sentences that stay focused on the distinction itself and its direct consequences.

The other 4 sentences create a clean logical sequence: definition -> logic -> mechanism -> consequence. Sentence 3 introduces a new actor (media) that doesn't fit this flow.

questions.question_text:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequencing of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the numbers as your answer.

  1. Each one personified a different aspect of good fortune.
  2. The others were versions of popular Buddhist gods, Hindu gods and Daoist gods.
  3. Seven popular Japanese deities, the Shichi Fukujin, were considered to bring good luck and happiness.
  4. Although they were included in the Shinto pantheon, only two of them, Daikoku and Ebisu, were indigenous Japanese gods.
questions.explanation_text:
The key to paragraph sequencing is finding the opener (introduces topic) and then following the logical chain of references.

From passage: "Seven popular Japanese deities, the Shichi Fukujin, were considered to bring good luck and happiness."

Step-by-step process:

Look for the sentence that introduces something new -> Sentence 3 introduces "seven Japanese deities" (no prior reference needed)

Follow pronouns and references -> "Each one" in sentence 1 must refer back to the seven deities -> so 1 comes after 3

Continue the chain -> Sentence 4 mentions "only two of them" were Japanese -> this explains more about the seven deities

Complete the thought -> "The others" in sentence 2 refers to the remaining five deities -> explains what the non-Japanese ones were

Elimination strategy:

Any sequence not starting with 3 -> wrong opener -> other sentences need something to refer back to

Sentence 1 before 3 -> pronoun error -> "Each one" has nothing to refer to

Sentence 2 before explaining the split -> logic gap -> "others" makes no sense without knowing the division first

Sentence 4 before 1 -> flow disruption -> jumps to specifics before explaining what each deity represents

Flow check: 3 (introduces topic) -> 1 (explains each deity's role) -> 4 (splits into Japanese vs foreign) -> 2 (explains the foreign ones)

The answer 3142 creates perfect logical flow with clear pronoun references.

questions.question_text:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequencing of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the numbers as your answer.

  1. Complex computational elements of the CNS are organized according to a "nested" hierarchic criterion; the organization is not permanent and can change dynamically from moment to moment as they carry out a computational task.
  2. Echolocation in bats exemplifies adaptation produced by natural selection; a function not produced by natural selection for its current use is exaptation -- feathers might have originally arisen in the context of selection for insulation.
  3. From a structural standpoint, consistent with exaptation, the living organism is organized as a complex of "Russian Matryoshka Dolls" -- smaller structures are contained within larger ones in multiple layers.
  4. The exaptation concept, and the Russian-doll organization concept of living beings deduced from studies on evolution of the various apparatuses in mammals, can be applied for the most complex human organ: the central nervous system (CNS).
questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "Echolocation in bats exemplifies adaptation produced by natural selection; a function not produced by natural selection for its current use is exaptation"

The thought process is: Start with basic concepts → Connect to CNS → Explain structure → Give specific details

Sentence 2 introduces adaptation vs exaptation with clear examples → Sentence 4 applies these concepts to CNS specifically → Sentence 3 explains the Russian doll structure → Sentence 1 gives specific CNS details

Most students get confused between starting with sentence 3 or 4, but here's the elimination strategy:

🟠 Starting with 3 → partial-truth → mentions Russian doll concept but doesn't explain what exaptation is first. You can't understand "consistent with exaptation" without knowing what exaptation means.

🟠 Starting with 4 → context-shift → jumps straight to CNS application without establishing the basic concepts first. The reader needs to understand adaptation/exaptation before applying them.

🔴 Starting with 1 → irrelevant → talks about CNS details without any context. Too specific to start a paragraph about evolutionary concepts.

🟢 Starting with 2 is correct → introduces fundamental concepts (adaptation/exaptation) with concrete examples, setting up the foundation for everything that follows.

The flow: Basic concepts (2) → Application to CNS (4) → Structural explanation (3) → Specific details (1)

Answer: 2431

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

The dominant hypotheses in modern science believe that language evolved to allow humans to exchange factual information about the physical world. But an alternative view is that language evolved, in modern humans at least, to facilitate social bonding. It increased our ancestors' chances of survival by enabling them to hunt more successfully or to cooperate more extensively. Language meant that things could be explained and that plans and past experiences could be shared efficiently.

options.label: A
options.text: Most believe that language originated from a need to articulate facts, but others think it emerged from the need to promote social cohesion and cooperation, thus enabling human survival.

options.label: B
options.text: From the belief that humans invented language to process factual information, scholars now think that language was the outcome of the need to ensure social cohesion and thus human survival.

options.label: C
options.text: Since its origin, language has been continuously evolving to higher forms, from being used to identify objects to ensuring human survival by enabling our ancestors to bond and cooperate.

options.label: D
options.text: Experts are challenging the narrow view of the origin of language, as being merely used to describe facts and label objects, to being necessary to promote more complex interactions among humans.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find the two main views about how language evolved. From passage: "The dominant hypotheses in modern science believe that language evolved to allow humans to exchange factual information about the physical world. But an alternative view is that language evolved... to facilitate social bonding."

The passage shows me two competing ideas:

  • Dominant view -> language evolved for sharing facts about the world
  • Alternative view -> language evolved for social bonding and cooperation

The key insight -> these are two current competing theories, not one replacing the other or evolving over time.

🟢 Option 1 -> correct -> captures both views accurately. "Most believe" = dominant hypotheses, "but others think" = alternative view. Shows both factual information theory AND social bonding theory.

🔴 Option 2 -> context-shift -> suggests scholars moved "from" one belief "now" to another. But passage shows these as two current competing views, not a historical shift.

🔴 Option 3 -> scope-error -> talks about "continuously evolving to higher forms" and progression. Passage doesn't discuss continuous evolution or stages - just presents two competing theories.

🟠 Option 4 -> context-shift + degree-error -> says experts are "challenging" one view. Passage doesn't show challenge or conflict, just presents both as existing hypotheses. Also adds judgment words like "narrow" and "merely" not in passage.

The confusion students face -> Options 2 and 4 seem tempting because they mention both theories, but they wrongly suggest one theory is replacing the other, when the passage shows them as competing current views.

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Brown et al. (2001) suggest that 'metabolic theory may provide a conceptual foundation for much of ecology just as genetic theory provides a foundation for much of evolutionary biology'. One of the successes of genetic theory is the diversity of theoretical approaches and models that have been developed and applied. A Web of Science (v. 5.9. Thomson Reuters) search on genetic* + theor* + evol* identifies more than 12000 publications between 2005 and 2012. Considering only the 10 most-cited papers within this 12000 publication set, genetic theory can be seen to focus on genome dynamics, phylogenetic inference, game theory and the regulation of gene expression. There is no one fundamental genetic equation, but rather a wide array of genetic models, ranging from simple to complex, with differing inputs and outputs, and divergent areas of application, loosely connected to each other through the shared conceptual foundation of heritable variation.

options.label: A
options.text: Genetic theory has a wide range of theoretical approaches and applications and Metabolic theory must have the same in the field of ecology.

options.label: B
options.text: Genetic theory has evolved to spawn a wide range of theoretical models and applications but Metabolic theory need not evolve in a similar manner in the field of ecology.

options.label: C
options.text: Genetic theory has a wide range of theoretical approaches and application and is foundational to evolutionary biology and Metabolic theory has the potential to do the same for ecology.

options.label: D
options.text: Genetic theory provides an example of how a range of theoretical approaches and applications can make a theory successful.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what it's really saying about both genetic theory and metabolic theory.

From passage: "Brown et al. (2001) suggest that 'metabolic theory may provide a conceptual foundation for much of ecology just as genetic theory provides a foundation for much of evolutionary biology'"

The passage structure: Shows genetic theory's success with diversity -> suggests metabolic theory might do similar for ecology.

Think process: Genetic theory works because it has many approaches -> Maybe metabolic theory can work the same way for ecology -> This is a suggestion, not a certainty.

🔴 Option 1 -> degree-error -> Says metabolic theory "must have the same" but passage only says it "may provide" - too strong and definitive

🔴 Option 2 -> contradicts main point -> Says metabolic theory "need not evolve in similar manner" but the whole passage suggests it could/should

🟠 Option 4 -> partial-truth -> Only talks about genetic theory as example but completely ignores the metabolic theory part, which is the main point

🟢 Option 3 is correct -> Captures both parts: genetic theory's success and metabolic theory's potential (not certainty) to do same for ecology

Key insight: The passage makes a comparison - genetic theory succeeded with diversity, so metabolic theory has potential to succeed similarly. Option 3 is the only one that captures both sides of this comparison with the right degree of certainty.

questions.question_text:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequencing of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the numbers as your answer.

  1. It advocated a conservative approach to antitrust enforcement that espouses faith in efficient markets and voiced suspicion regarding the merits of judicial intervention to correct anticompetitive practices.
  2. Many industries have consistently gained market share, the lion's share - without any official concern; the most successful technology companies have grown into veritable titans, on the premise that they advance 'public interest'.
  3. That the new anticompetitive risks posed by tech giants like Google, Facebook, and Amazon, necessitate new legal solutions could be attributed to the dearth of enforcement actions against monopolies and the few cases challenging mergers in the USA.
  4. The criterion of 'consumer welfare standard' and the principle that antitrust law should serve consumer interests and that it should protect competition rather than individual competitors was an antitrust law introduced by, and named after, the 'Chicago school'.
questions.explanation_text:
Step-by-step thought process:

First, identify what each sentence talks about:

  • Sentence 1: Says "It advocated..." -> needs something before it to define what "it" is
  • Sentence 2: Shows consequences -> industries gaining market share without concern
  • Sentence 3: Calls for new solutions -> because current enforcement is weak
  • Sentence 4: Defines what the Chicago school antitrust law is

From passage: "The criterion of 'consumer welfare standard'... was an antitrust law introduced by, and named after, the 'Chicago school'"

The logical flow: Definition -> Approach -> Consequences -> Need for change

Start with sentence 4 (defines the law) -> sentence 1 (explains what "it" advocated) -> sentence 2 (shows results) -> sentence 3 (calls for new solutions)

Why students get confused: They might start with sentence 1 because it sounds like an opening, but "it" needs a reference first. Or they might put sentence 3 first because it mentions current problems.

Elimination process:

  • Any sequence starting with 1 is wrong -> "it" has no reference
  • Any sequence starting with 2 or 3 is wrong -> jumps into consequences/solutions without context
  • Only sequence starting with 4 makes sense -> gives the foundation first

The answer is 4123 -> Definition of Chicago school law -> Its conservative approach -> Resulting market concentration -> Need for new solutions.
